the problem

Your builds keep downloading the same dependencies.

Across CI runners and developer machines, repeat downloads slow builds, consume bandwidth, and become a hard stop when the network is disconnected.

Start the setup tutorial Open console

A step-by-step walkthrough — download the client, open a temporary shell, and wire up pip, uv, npm, Git, apt and Docker.

the waiting

Repeat downloads stall builds

Large images and wheels cross the same network again while machines wait for work they have already done.

the sprawl

A cache for every ecosystem

Separate services for containers, Python, Node and system packages multiply configuration, maintenance and failure points.

the wall

One missing package stops the build

Disconnected environments cannot reach upstream registries, so an uncached dependency can stop the entire pipeline.

one cache, every ecosystem

Fetch once. Keep repeat package requests local.

Point your existing package clients at pkgreg. It fills on demand, serves cached content from your infrastructure, and combines concurrent misses into one upstream transfer.

01

Local after the first pull

Once an artifact is cached, repeat requests are served from your infrastructure instead of the public registry.

02

One fetch, shared as it arrives

When several machines request the same uncached artifact together, pkgreg opens one upstream stream and serves them all.

03

One service for the build stack

Containers, Python, Node, system packages, Git and generic artifacts share one process and a consistent project setup.

LOCALcached artifact → served from your infrastructure
ONCEuncached artifact → one upstream stream shared by concurrent callers
VALIDfailed or incomplete downloads are never committed as cached content

versioned cache state

Checkpoint the cache without stopping builds.

Capture the cached content and its ledger while the service keeps running. Every checkpoint becomes an auditable restore point and a source for air-gap transfer.

  1. captureCheckpointRecord exactly what the cache holds while package traffic continues.
  2. transferExport the deltaStage only the cache changes needed on the other side.
  3. recoverRoll backRestore a known checkpoint when a build environment must be reproduced.

built for disconnected networks

Bring the cache with you. Keep cached builds running.

Export a checkpoint delta, move it through your approved transfer process, and import it on the far side. Package clients keep using the cache with upstream access disabled.

  1. moveCarry the deltaCopy the exported cache changes to approved removable media or an internal transfer path.
  2. importLoad it offlineImport the checkpoint on the disconnected host and start the cache in offline mode.
  3. serveBuild cache-onlyCached dependencies resolve normally. An uncached request fails clearly instead of attempting upstream access.

Six ecosystems · one service

One cache service for the tools your builds already use.

All six roles share one address — :8443 — including the apt and apk forward proxy.Five HTTPS roles share :8443; apt and apk use the :3142 forward proxy. Run pkgreg-client to open a verified temporary shell for pip, uv, npm, Git, files and the apt/apk proxy. Nothing is installed, and exiting the shell restores the previous environment. Docker runs through a separate daemon that cannot read that shell, so it has its own section in the tutorial.

containersDocker Hub · GHCR · Quay

Container images

Cache images from Docker Hub, GHCR and Quay. Pulls, builds and CI each need the address passed to the daemon differently.

new to pkgreg? start here

Download the client before copying commands.

The pip, npm, apt, Git and files examples run inside the temporary pkgreg-client shell. The client verifies the remote cache, exposes it on localhost, and configures only the child shell. No administrator access or permanent CA installation is needed. The tutorial walks through it in three steps, then covers Docker and shared CI hosts, which each work differently.

operate it from one place

See what is cached. Measure the value. Control every transfer.

The console is part of the binary — no separate service, no container, nothing extra to deploy. Six pages follow what a project actually goes through, a project switcher scopes all of them, and an activity rail shows running jobs and live transfers from any page.

Open the console
  • Overview — requests over time split by where each one was answered, disk pressure against the eviction floor, live activity.
  • Cache — what is stored, by ecosystem and by package, and how much of it has gone cold.
  • Connect — the exact commands for this instance, the certificate and its fingerprint.
  • Sources — where misses go, and which upstream is slow or failing.
  • Transfer — checkpoint, export, import, roll back, warm from a lockfile.
  • Admin — quotas, garbage collection, accounts and the audit log.

Every chart has a table view beside it, and gaps in a chart mean “not recorded”, never “nothing happened”. Running without a browser surface at all is one flag: pkgreg serve --headless keeps the API, metrics and health endpoints up and answers 404 everywhere else.
